notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [א] ״שֶׁמַּגַּעַת עַד כִּסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד״, הוּא רְפוּאַת הַקּוֹדֵם וּמַה שֶּׁעָבַר גַּם כֵּן
notes.body_html: Yoma 86a: “R’ Levi said: Great is teshuvah, for it reaches the Throne of Glory, as it says, ‘Return, O Israel, unto [ad] Hashem your God’ (Hoshea 14:2).” R’ Tzadok: the word ad (“up to”) indicates a teshuvah that ascends to the very root of the soul at the Throne — i.e. the rectification of the past, not merely the future. Maharal on "until the Throne of Glory." Netivos Olam, Netiv HaTeshuvah ch. 2 (§13 in Sefaria's segmentation), treats the Yoma statement itself: "גדולה תשובה שמגעת עד כסא הכבוד." Elsewhere in the same chapter (§16, §22), the Maharal explains that teshuvah removes the sinner from the material level in which sin took hold and returns him to a higher, separated level. Because teshuvah reaches the Kisei HaKavod and itself precedes the created world, it belongs to a plane above the ordinary causal order of sin and consequence. This gives conceptual force to R' Tzadok's distinction between simple forgiveness and tikkun ha-kodem: the Kisei is not merely a very high place to which the penitent climbs; it is the level from which the soul's created history can be re-grounded. The Maharal's formulation also dovetails with R' Tzadok's language of return to the shoresh. Teshuvah is a "return" because the person ceases to be fixed at the material level defined by the sin and is restored to the higher source from which his neshama proceeds. Hence Yoma's "ad kisei ha-kavod" is not rhetorical praise but a statement about the metaphysical reach of teshuvah.

notes.body_html: Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 43: the source R’ Tzadok cites for the teaching that the three levels of the soul — nefesh, ruach, and neshamah — are drawn from the three lower worlds: nefesh from Asiyah (the world of the spheres, galgalim), ruach from Yetzirah (the world of the angels), and neshamah from Beriah (the world of the Throne of Glory). Because Beriah, the world of the Throne, is “mostly good,” the neshamah — which corresponds to the thought of the mind — remains essentially pure, as we declare each morning, “the soul You placed within me is pure.” The corruption of sin therefore lodges not in the neshamah but in the heart, the seat of the yetzer.

notes.body_html: Bamidbar 15:39: the verse of tzitzis — “וְהָיָה לָכֶם לְצִיצִת וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ וּזְכַרְתֶּם אֶת כָּל מִצְוֹת ה׳ וַעֲשִׂיתֶם אֹתָם, וְלֹא תָתוּרוּ אַחֲרֵי לְבַבְכֶם וְאַחֲרֵי עֵינֵיכֶם אֲשֶׁר אַתֶּם זֹנִים אַחֲרֵיהֶם” — “and it shall be for you as a fringe, that you may look upon it and remember all the commandments of Hashem and perform them; and you shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes, after which you go astray.” Rashi explains that the heart and the eyes are “the spies of the body” (meraglim la-guf), the go-betweens for sin: the eye sees, the heart covets, and the body commits the transgression. R’ Tzadok builds on this that the root of sin lies in the heart — the dwelling-place of the yetzer hara — and hence that the thought of teshuvah in the heart is the beginning of rectification.

notes.body_html: Bereishis Rabbah 34:10: “The wicked are in the control of their heart, but the righteous — their heart is in their control,” each proven from verses. R’ Tzadok infers that the mind (not the heart) is the person’s essence: in the righteous the heart’s desire follows the mind’s clear thought, whereas in the wicked the mind is dragged after the heart. Tanya on the mind-heart structure. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 12 (12:5 in Sefaria's segmentation), states the classic principle: "המוח שליט על הלב ... בתולדתו וטבע יצירתו" — the mind rules over the heart by the nature of man's creation. Even when desire remains alive in the heart, a person can prevent it from passing from potential into actual thought, speech, and deed by directing the will in the mind. Chapter 30 repeats the practical consequence: a person is expected to restrain the spirit of desire in his heart because the mind is naturally given governing power. This is an exceptionally close parallel to R' Tzadok's use of Bereishis Rabbah that "the righteous have their heart in their control." R' Tzadok goes farther in identifying the clear mind as the person's essential human point, while the heart is the seat where desire and the yetzer are felt. Tanya supplies the avodah-psychology: righteousness does not require that every unwanted feeling disappear before one can be called a tzaddik in the relevant behavioral sense; it requires that the Divine-directed mind govern what the heart is allowed to express. This also clarifies why teshuvah can begin in a single true turn of da'as even before every emotional residue has been healed.

notes.body_html: Bava Basra 16a: “The Holy One created the yetzer hara, and created the Torah as its antidote [tavlin, lit. spice].” Kiddushin 30b: “If this repulsive one [the yetzer] meets you, drag him to the study-hall: if he is stone he will dissolve, if iron he will shatter.” R’ Tzadok: Torah is the mind’s wisdom that masters the heart’s yetzer. A Chassidic reading of Torah as the yetzer's tavlin. R' Tzadok's emphasis that the "help" from Above arrives through Torah belongs to a broad Chassidic pattern: the Torah does not merely suppress the lower force; it can season and redirect it. Tzidkas HaTzadik §240, already cited nearby, states this explicitly. Compare Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 39, where even Torah itself can descend temporarily into kelipas nogah through ulterior motive and then "returns with" the person when he does teshuvah. The two directions illuminate one another: Torah enters the arena of the mixed human heart in order to refine it, and teshuvah can in turn liberate Torah that had been entangled with the person's mixed motive. This reciprocal movement fits the word tavlin, "spice," better than a simple weapon-metaphor. A spice works *within* the food; likewise Torah enters the powers of the person and changes their taste. The Izhbitz school repeatedly stresses that the human task is not to pretend the yetzer does not exist but to subject every power to birur until its true place in ratzon Hashem is disclosed.

notes.body_html: Shabbos 119b: Reish Lakish taught in the name of R’ Yehudah Nesi’ah that “the world endures only for the sake of the breath [hevel] of the schoolchildren” — the Torah of little children who bear no sin. R’ Tzadok applies this to Moshe’s fear of the angels — “lest they consume me with the breath of their mouths”: the sinless breath of the angels would overpower the breath of one who has sinned.

notes.body_html: Zohar (on “her husband is known in the gates,” Mishlei 31:23): “noda ba’she’arim — each one according to what he apprehends [measures, me’sha’er] in his heart”; the Divine “Husband” is “known” to each soul in the measure of that soul’s own vessel. R’ Tzadok: hence the singular “your God” — the graded, individual apprehension of the “world of separation” (the Throne, Beriah). Izhbitz-Radzin and the individualized measure of Divine apprehension. Beis Yaakov, Vayechi 24:1, emphasizes that the illumination of bechirah and da'as is not identical in every soul or at every time: what is "day" for one soul may be "night" for another, and even within a single Jew the clarity of da'as can expand and contract. The avodah established in the clear hour must therefore carry the person through periods when the light of choice and understanding is hidden. This is closely related to "לפום מה דמשער בלביה": the Divine truth is one, but the vessel through which it is presently received is particular. The point protects R' Tzadok's language from being read as relativism. Each soul has its own shiur, not its own Torah. The same Hashem is "known in the gates" according to the measure of the heart, while halachic obligation remains objective. The individualized apprehension concerns the depth, taste, and inner recognition with which the common Torah is lived.

R’ Tzadok cites this for the principle that in the revealed apprehension of Godhead there is a genuine difference among individual souls, each one tasting according to his portion — as opposed to emunah, the concealed faith shared alike by all Israel.

notes.body_html:
Shabbos 97a: “Israel are believers, the children of believers” — and one who suspects the worthy is stricken; faith is the shared root of Knesses Yisrael. R’ Tzadok: because faith operates in “concealment,” it admits no gradation — every Jew equally believes; this equal-in-all concealment is David’s rung of teshuvah. Izhbitz-Radzin on emunah that remains when da'as is concealed. Beis Yaakov, Vayechi 24:1, explains that there are times when "אור הבחירה" and the person's felt da'as are hidden; therefore Chazal fixed Krias Shema and tefillah each morning so that the prior acceptance of Malchus Shamayim surrounds and carries him even through the later hours of concealment. This gives a practical form to R' Tzadok's distinction between emunah and revealed apprehension. The equal root-faith of Israel is not a lesser substitute for knowledge but the covenantal hold that persists when individualized spiritual clarity recedes.

That is why David's rung can be associated with concealment without being a defect. Davidic emunah means the ability to remain attached precisely where the visible proof is absent — the spiritual condition in which teshuvah begins, before the person's past has been openly transfigured.

notes.body_html: Divrei HaYamim I 29:23: “וַיֵּשֶׁב שְׁלֹמֹה עַל כִּסֵּא ה׳ לְמֶלֶךְ תַּחַת דָּוִיד אָבִיו וַיַּצְלַח, וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ אֵלָיו כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל” — “And Shlomo sat upon the Throne of Hashem as king in place of David his father, and he prospered, and all Israel heeded him.” Scripture uniquely calls Israel’s royal throne “the Throne of Hashem,” for the kingship of the House of David is the earthly embodiment of the kingship of Heaven — as the Gemara puts it, “earthly kingship is a likeness of the heavenly kingship” (Berachos 58a). R’ Tzadok therefore assigns to Shlomo the rung of reaching the Throne of Glory itself, in contrast to David’s rung — the teshuvah that rises from the concealment shared by all Israel. Maharal and the symbolism of the Kisei. Gevuros Hashem ch. 70, in explaining the seven things created before the world, identifies the Kisei HaKavod with absolute elevation and with malchus: "כסא" signifies kingship, the level at which Hashem is revealed as exalted over the created order. Teshuvah and the Kisei are both pre-worldly realities in that sugya. R' Tzadok's assignment of Shlomo to the second rung can therefore be read with precision: "וישב שלמה על כסא ה'" is not merely a royal metaphor but an earthly appearance of the level to which teshuvah reaches. For David the forgiveness is real while its final vindication remains hidden; under Shlomo, the gates open and the truth of David's past is publicly disclosed. The transition from David to Shlomo thus mirrors the movement from concealed teshuvah to the Kisei's revealed malchus.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §68): “All the services of the body’s limbs, and the mitzvos performed through them, are only to straighten the heart; and the essence is the heart, for there is the dwelling-place of Hashem — as the Sages said (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2), ‘the Holy One is the heart of Israel,’ as it says, ‘the Rock of my heart’ (Tehillim 73:26).” This is precisely the image §2-5 invokes — “a king is likened to the heart in the body”: the limbs (the nation) exist to serve and actualize the heart (the king), the single root-organ that is the seat of vitality and of the bond with God, and from which all the rest draws its life.

notes.body_html: Eicha 2:9: “טָבְעוּ בָאָרֶץ שְׁעָרֶיהָ, אִבַּד וְשִׁבַּר בְּרִיחֶיהָ, מַלְכָּהּ וְשָׂרֶיהָ בַגּוֹיִם אֵין תּוֹרָה, גַּם נְבִיאֶיהָ לֹא מָצְאוּ חָזוֹן מֵה׳” — “Her gates have sunk into the ground, He has ruined and shattered her bars; her king and her officers are among the nations, there is no Torah; her prophets, too, find no vision from Hashem.” Rashi, citing the Sages (Sotah 9a), explains that the Temple gates David had wrought sank into the earth rather than fall to the enemy — “they were the handiwork of David, and therefore the enemies had no power over them”; and Eichah Rabbah adds that the gates had once done honor to the Aron, saying “lift up your heads, O gates” (Tehillim 24:7). R’ Tzadok reads this as the mark of David’s rung: his yiras shamayim, the root of Knesses Yisrael, gives the nations no purchase, so his handiwork can never come under their rule.

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 8:21: “וְעָבַר בָּהּ נִקְשֶׁה וְרָעֵב, וְהָיָה כִי יִרְעַב וְהִתְקַצַּף וְקִלֵּל בְּמַלְכּוֹ וּבֵאלֹהָיו וּפָנָה לְמָעְלָה” — “And he shall pass through it hard-pressed and hungry; and it shall be, when he is hungry, that he shall rage and curse his king and his god, and turn his face upward.” Rashi explains that this speaks of those who forsake the Holy One and rely on the kings of Egypt: when famine and siege overtake them, “he curses the calves and the baalim they had worshipped, and turns upward to beseech Hashem — who will not listen, for the decree has been sealed.” R’ Tzadok contrasts this fickle fear with Israel’s: the nations cling to their god only in good times and blaspheme in distress, whereas Israel’s yirah endures “whether in His goodness or in affliction,” and a Jew, when he is stricken, does not “cry out in complaint” (Rosh Hashanah 4a).

notes.body_html: Tehillim 23:4: “גַּם כִּי אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת לֹא אִירָא רָע כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי, שִׁבְטְךָ וּמִשְׁעַנְתֶּךָ הֵמָּה יְנַחֲמֻנִי” — “Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff — they comfort me.” In its plain sense (Rashi; Metzudat David), David declares that even when passing through places dark as death’s shadow he fears no harm, for Hashem is at his side, and even the “rod” of affliction is for his good and consoles him. notes.body_html: Shemos 15:25: at Marah — “וַיִּצְעַק אֶל ה׳ וַיּוֹרֵהוּ ה׳ עֵץ וַיַּשְׁלֵךְ אֶל הַמַּיִם וַיִּמְתְּקוּ הַמָּיִם, שָׁם שָׂם לוֹ חֹק וּמִשְׁפָּט וְשָׁם נִסָּהוּ” — “and he cried out to Hashem, and Hashem showed him a tree; he cast it into the water, and the water turned sweet. notes.body_html: Shemos 6:7: “וְלָקַחְתִּי אֶתְכֶם לִי לְעָם וְהָיִיתִי לָכֶם לֵאלֹקִים, וִידַעְתֶּם כִּי אֲנִי ה׳ אֱלֹקֵיכֶם הַמּוֹצִיא אֶתְכֶם מִתַּחַת סִבְלוֹת מִצְרָיִם” — “And I will take you to Me for a people, and I will be to you a God; and you shall know that I am Hashem your God who brings you out from under the burdens of Egypt” — the second of the four expressions of redemption. R’ Tzadok fastens on the word “ve-lakachti [and I will take]”: a “taking,” with a person, is total and essence-changing — like betrothal, an utter acquisition — and so the word “lekach [taking]” in Mishlei (“let the wise hear and add lekach”) denotes the way Torah-wisdom effects a change in the very root of a person’s knowledge and will, which is the healing of the past.
